content: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are estimated to occur in approximately 15% of clean surgeries and 30% of contaminated surgeries. One proposed method to prevent SSIs is the use of plastic adhesive drapes during surgery. These drapes are intended to shield the surgical wound from microorganisms present on the surrounding skin. However, non-randomized studies have reported inconsistent findings regarding the effectiveness of this approach. A systematic review was conducted to provide evidence-based guidance for clinical practice. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of adhesive drapes on surgical site infection rates, as well as their effects on cost, mortality, and morbidity. For the fourth update of this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL, with the most recent search conducted in March 2015. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the use of plastic adhesive drapes to no drapes. These drapes could be used alone or in combination with woven (fabric) or disposable (paper) drapes. Studies involving ring drapes were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. No new studies were identified in this fourth update. The review included five studies with a total of 3,082 participants comparing plastic adhesive drapes to no drapes, and two studies with 1,113 participants comparing iodine-impregnated adhesive drapes to no drapes. The findings revealed that a significantly higher proportion of patients in the plastic adhesive drape group developed surgical site infections compared to those in the no-drape group (risk ratio [RR] 1.23, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02 to 1.48, P = 0.03). In contrast, iodine-impregnated adhesive drapes did not significantly affect the rate of surgical site infections (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.66, P = 0.89). The length of hospital stay was similar between the adhesive drape and non-adhesive drape groups. The authors concluded that there is no evidence from the seven included trials to support the use of plastic adhesive drapes for reducing surgical site infection rates. In fact, there is some evidence suggesting that these drapes may increase the risk of infection. Further research, including trials with blinded outcome assessments, may be warranted to explore the effects of adhesive drapes on surgical site infections across different wound classifications.
